repos.title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
repos.paper_summary: SpecCompact accelerates context compaction for LLM agents by drafting each summary slot in parallel with a fine-tuned 0.6B drafter (Qwen3-0.6B) and verifying each proposed line with the target model, which accepts the line or writes a local replacement. The six slots follow OpenClaw's schema (Goal, Constraints, Progress, Key Decisions, Next Steps, Critical Context). Verification is binary: a line is accepted when the normalized positive probability is at least 0.7. System optimizations include shared-prefix caching, draft buffering, and line-aware stopping. Against Hermes-style summarization, compaction speedups are 2.04–5.63× across AppWorld, τ3 and LongBench inputs, with Gemma4-31B-IT giving the larger gains. Downstream effects vary by model. With Gemma4, SpecCompact lowers AppWorld Normal TGC from 57.74 to 54.76%. With Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, it raises AppWorld Normal TGC from 28.57 to 33.33%. On RULER, Gemma4 at 8k drops from 71.00 (Target-self) to 66.50. The authors state that SpecCompact does not consistently match target-model summarization in accuracy. Limitations include a 19.6-point lower draft acceptance rate for Qwen3.5 and speedups that shrink on that model. A user study in Hermes reports a median compaction speedup of 8.68×, with latency falling from 63.74 to 7.28 seconds.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Summary slots generated independently can still retain needed information, which motivates parallel compaction.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Independent slot generation scores 4.73 against 4.44 for monolithic generation across 100 trajectories.

digest_headlines.heading: SpecCompact
digest_headlines.headline: SpecCompact drafts six slots in parallel with a fine-tuned small model, with the target verifying and repairing each line.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: SpecCompact reaches 2.04–5.63x compaction speedups over Hermes, with downstream effects that depend on the target model.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers compaction execution and semantic speculation, the two areas SpecCompact combines.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: SpecCompact shows no consistent accuracy advantage over target summarization, and better drafter alignment may help.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: SpecCompact cuts compaction latency with accuracy trade-offs, and a native Hermes user study confirms the latency benefit.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the drafter prompt, the six slot contracts, and the target verification prompt with its message structure.

repos.title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?
repos.paper_summary: CompressionBench is a terminal task in which coding agents compress LLMs autonomously. Each agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, GPU, pinned runtime, and eight-hour budget, and must output compressed weights plus the inference code that runs them. Six agents each attempted six tasks (three source models, two storage limits each). Agents search using a perplexity-ratio reward. The frozen artifact is then verified on held-out likelihood, storage, and GSM8K, HumanEval, and TriviaQA accuracy, which must retain 80% of BF16. Of 36 submissions, 29 pass. The lowest-PPL passing artifact per task averages a 3.4% PPL increase over BF16 and 77.33% accuracy versus 79.56% for BF16. Agents lowered PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage. Complete-model feedback reversed 17 of 79 prior local rankings, and likelihood alone missed generation and execution failures. Limitations: each benchmark uses fifty questions, decode speed is excluded from the reward, and the link to recursive self-improvement, whether compressed models can perform later compression, is untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Compression becomes a terminal task: agents build compressed LLMs and inference code under a storage limit.

digest_headlines.heading: Compression as a Terminal Task
digest_headlines.headline: Verification scores only models that fit both storage limits and retain 80% of BF16 accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Empirical Study
digest_headlines.headline: Twenty-nine of thirty-six agent-built models pass verification, and the best per task averages a 3.4% perplexity increase.

digest_headlines.heading: How Agents Improve Compression
digest_headlines.headline: At nearly fixed storage, agents lowered perplexity in 21 of 24 revisions by refining quantizers or precision.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work supplies agent benchmarks and compression methods; this paper combines them into one agent-built model task.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agent compression needs numerical design, experimental judgment, and validation; whether compressed models retain this ability is untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists evaluation protocol, search stopping, full measurements, pilot storage studies, and controlled ablations.

repos.title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
repos.paper_summary: LongBanana is a benchmark of 90 expert-designed, expert-verified tasks for synthesizing one image from many reference images, with 4,670 atomic checklist items. Tasks average about 32 references and include hard-negative references that must be excluded. Each task is converted into an entity–relation graph, and items are scored on Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction by LongBananaEval, an agentic judge that calls tools such as OCR and counting. Reviewers labeled 46,700 item judgments; a 15% double-labeled subset reached 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. On output-level Overall scores, LongBananaEval reaches Pearson 0.8707, versus 0.8413 for a single-pass VLM judge. For generation, the paper compares direct prompting, agent harnesses, and RPR workflows, with Nano Banana 2 as the image generator. The best system, OpenClaw + RPR, scores 78.4 average and 47.8 P@70%, against 74.6 and 35.6 for PD-Direct, a baseline given the construction graph. RPR gains depend on the harness, and the paper notes it can introduce drift.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-reference image generation errors are provenance failures that holistic realism scores cannot localize.

digest_headlines.heading: The LongBanana Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: LongBanana contains 90 cases across a 3-by-3 taxonomy, each scored through atomic graph-derived checklist items.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Nano Banana 2 under OpenClaw with RPR scores 78.4 overall, above the 68.4 of full-prompt direct generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agentic workflows reach broader success than a fixed privileged schedule, and checklist scores localize failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: Funding comes from two Guangdong programs and KlingAI Research, and the authors declare no other competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, benchmark construction details, scorer and label quality statistics, extra experiments, and release safeguards.

repos.title: Visual Token Routing: Learning to keep tokens that matter
repos.paper_summary: Visual Token Routing (VTR) is a joint training framework that teaches a vision-language computer-use agent to keep only the visual tokens it needs for its next action. A lightweight spatio-temporal router, a three-layer MLP with 23.3M parameters, reads each image region across the current and previous 10 screenshots and decides whether to keep its token. Kept tokens are scaled by their keep probability so the router receives gradients. Training uses a dual objective: the router minimizes the expected fraction of kept tokens, while an adaptive multiplier keeps the degradation, measured against full-history and anchor-only reference models, at or below 10% of the full history's improvement. Applied to Qwen3.5-2B, VTR matches the dense model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction with 2.5-5.8× fewer visual tokens, and reduces inference cost by up to 3.3× and prefill time by up to 2.9×. On OSWorld it scores 18.1, against 9.4 for H.264 token selection, 5.3 for pixel-diff, and 4.9 for a frozen router. Limitations: results cover one base model and three evaluation settings, and the router is initialized from heuristic labels that use SAM segmentation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Computer-use agents spend thousands of visual tokens per screenshot, and most of them do not affect the next action.

digest_headlines.heading: Visual Token Routing
digest_headlines.headline: A spatio-temporal router samples keep-or-drop gates per visual token and is trained jointly with the model under an accuracy target.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen3.5-2B is trained on desktop and game data and compared with lower resolution, pixel-difference, codec-based, and frozen-router baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: VTR matches full-resolution scores on OSWorld, CUA-World, and game clicks with 2.5-5.8 times fewer visual tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier token reduction methods fix the kept-token count in advance or train their selector apart from the action model.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: VTR lets computer-use agents process only the visual tokens they need, cutting inference cost by up to 3.3 times.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training data, router architecture, joint-training hyperparameters, baseline settings, evaluation protocols, and extra result tables.

repos.title: Trainspotting: Learning Object-Centric 3D Reconstruction from Found Photos
repos.paper_summary: Trainspotting is a dataset of 12,068 objects and 311,886 photos from Wikimedia Commons, reconstructed to provide camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks, along with a fine-tuned feedforward model, Spotter, built from VGGT-Ω. Each object is reconstructed by filtering photos with SAM3 prompts, matching image pairs with RoMa v2 under confidence, cycle-consistency, and epipolar checks, running COLMAP, selecting views by covisibility, and running Cas-DiffMVS depth verified against MoGe-2. Spotter is fine-tuned on training objects with a camera, depth, and point loss, with 15% replay from BlendedMVS, Hypersim, and uCO3D. On 1,000 held-out objects, camera-pose AUC@30 rises from 25.0 to 81.2 over VGGT-Ω, and on NAVI in-the-wild from 19 to 76. Depth AbsRel falls from 0.201 to 0.071. Performance on conventional benchmarks is largely unchanged. Limitations: the regime labels come from LLM classification and are approximate, and structure from motion succeeds for only 85% of objects.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Public archives hold many found photos of one object, but feedforward reconstruction models are trained mostly on single-session captures.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing object datasets record each object in one capture, and internet photo reconstructions cover mostly scenes.

digest_headlines.heading: The Trainspotting Dataset
digest_headlines.headline: Language-model classification of Wikimedia Commons categories yields 12,068 rigid objects, each labeled fixed, roaming, or instance-pooled.

digest_headlines.heading: Pseudo-Ground Truth via Reconstruction
digest_headlines.headline: A dense-matching pipeline with geometric checks recovers camera poses, depth, and masks for each object as pseudo-ground truth.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning lifts held-out camera-pose score at the 30-degree threshold from 25.0 to 81.2 and depth inlier ratio from 28.1 to 53.3.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Variation in how an object is photographed, not only dataset scale, is what the base models lacked.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists category counts, rejected categories, pipeline yields, matcher comparison, thresholds, training, and evaluation details.

repos.title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
repos.paper_summary: ServerBench is a benchmark for how well LLM coding agents design complete, specialized LLM serving systems under a shared economic objective: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost, which the authors call "dollars per dollar." Agents start from a minimal Transformers server, have an 8-hour development budget, and their submissions are rebuilt in a fresh deployment and replayed on held-out seeds. Workloads are replays of recorded coding-agent sessions with shared prefixes, multi-turn structure, and parallel subagent branches, and latency targets are the p90 TTFT and TPOT of a frozen SGLang reference. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments (Gemma E4B, Qwen3.5 9B, Qwen3.8 27B INT4), 22 of 33 runs produced verified systems and 13 exceeded the strongest baseline. Claude Sonnet 5.5 scored 2.97 on Gemma E4B, 4.87× the vLLM reference. The authors report three findings: high-value designs raise capacity before adding load, agents interpret feedback better when tests use workload-relevant inputs, and verification must cover the execution paths that optimizations add. Limitations include one coding-trace source, closed-loop rather than open-loop replay, and single runs per agent-deployment pair.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: ServerBench asks coding agents to build complete LLM serving systems and scores them by latency-qualified value per GPU dollar.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks test kernels, patches, or servers under preset conditions, lacking stateful workloads and cost-based objectives.

digest_headlines.heading: ServerBench
digest_headlines.headline: Each task fixes the model, GPU allocation, and workload, and scores verified systems by dollars per dollar of qualified token value.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Claude Sonnet 5.5 reaches 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, and 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Substantial gains come with uneven delivery, pointing to three priorities for agent-built serving systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover three deployments and one trace source, and closed-loop replay with correlational analysis limits generalization and causal claims.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Recorded sessions are reconstructed without original content, generated code runs in isolated environments, and review does not prove safety.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists deployment calibration, replay records, verification settings, integrity review, controlled comparisons, and finding-guided experiments.

repos.title: Context-Aware Autoregressive Image Generation for Emerging Reasoning Properties
repos.paper_summary: Saccade AR (SAR) is a training-free, inference-time change to autoregressive image generation: at each step it ranks still-uncommitted token positions by cosine similarity to the prompt's conditioning embedding and commits the most relevant ones first. It is applied to patch-wise MaskGen (MaskGen-L, MaskGen-XL) and scale-wise Infinity (Infinity-2B, Infinity-8B) by decoding the final scale in M=16 groups. On GenEval, SAR raises Overall pass rate over random order for every model; for Infinity-8B, from 80.63% to 81.34%, and for MaskGen-L, from 53.94% to 57.49%. On a new 2,000-prompt long-prompt benchmark scored by Gemini 2.5 Pro on a 1–5 scale, SAR raises the average for Infinity-8B from 2.92 to 3.42. On MJHQ-30K FID, SAR is reported as statistically tied with random order. The DPG-Bench per-category results are mixed. Limitations: the long-prompt benchmark relies on a single VLM judge, the qualitative "reasoning" claims rest on a few visualized examples, and the paper does not establish that the ordering causes the reasoning behavior.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed or random generation orders can miss spatial structure, so the authors propose Saccade AR (SAR), a context-aware order.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior image autoregressive methods use raster, random, or scale-wise orders that are fixed in advance or chosen stochastically.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Context-aware ordering scores still-masked positions by similarity to the conditioning anchor and commits the top positions each step.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Context-aware ordering raises text-to-image and long-prompt reasoning scores on both model families, while FID stays tied with random ordering.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Across 8 checkpoints from four model families, context-aware ordering improves prompt alignment and reasoning, adds no parameters, and keeps aesthetic quality.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The authors thank the Office of Naval Research for grants supporting their Johns Hopkins University authors.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation details, class-conditional ImageNet results, a scale-wise retraining ablation, and inference latency.

repos.title: GFlowQEC: Generative Flow Networks that Learn to Sample Quantum LDPC Codes
repos.paper_summary: GFlowQEC is a generative flow network (GFlowNet) that proposes quantum LDPC codes. To the authors' knowledge, it is the first GFlowNet for quantum code design. It builds a lifted-product code one group element per slot and is trained with trajectory balance, so each code is sampled with probability proportional to a power of its failure-exponent score. The policy is trained once on scores from 42 earlier runs, then frozen. At 180 physical qubits, ranking ten policy draws per paid call finds 2.4 and 2.8 times as many new top-scoring codes, inequivalent to training codes, as tuned parallel tempering at noise biases γ = ±1. It finds over 3.5 times as many as a supervised screen. A screen ranking a hundred random candidates per call beats the policy. Soft Q-learning does as well at one bias and better at the other. Limitations: the gain is in codes found per budget, not the best code, since no code beats those from Bayesian optimisation, reinforcement learning or LLM searches. Scores use code distances only, with no decoder, and stored data and training are uncounted.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Good quantum codes are rare and each evaluation is costly, so a learned proposer may yield more good codes per call.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior searches include strong simple baselines, and GFlowNets have so far been applied to circuits rather than codes.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Lifted-product codes over a 36-element group give 180 physical qubits from ten group elements.

digest_headlines.heading: Search Space and Oracle
digest_headlines.headline: Codes are scored by a failure exponent from their distances, with a top-scoring threshold of 10.0 at bias plus or minus one.

digest_headlines.heading: GFlowQEC
digest_headlines.headline: GFlowQEC builds each tuple one slot at a time and trains on stored scores with no new oracle calls.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The policy is compared with tuned parallel tempering, a supervised screen, soft Q-learning and other searches at matched budgets.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: The policy finds 2.4 and 2.8 times as many inequivalent top-scoring codes as tuned parallel tempering; a screen wins at a hundred draws.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The lead holds per paid call but vanishes per CPU second of exact ladders.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A frozen policy finds more inequivalent top-scoring codes per paid call, but circuit-level noise remains untested.

repos.title: Open-HumanScale: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
repos.paper_summary: Open-HumanScale is an open recipe for pretraining robot policies on egocentric human video at up to 50,000 hours, released with the Open-HumanScale-50K corpus of 35.9 million curated clips annotated with hand motion and language. Clips are filtered for hand visibility and motion stability, then mapped to a shared bimanual end-effector action space. In closed-loop simulation with a common post-training protocol, the authors report a log-linear relation between pretraining hours and out-of-distribution success, with steeper curves when task and scene diversity grow with hours. HumanWAM-Vanilla, pretrained only on human data, reaches 92.08% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random after robot post-training. HumanWAM-Goal, which adds visual-goal conditioning and joint human-robot pretraining, reaches 92.70% and 84.60% on those settings, an 88.65% average. On physical robots, adding 45.9k human hours to a 14.6k-hour robot corpus raises zero-shot mean success over 20 tasks from 20.0% to 30.5%. The action space excludes locomotion, and the in-context learning evidence here is qualitative.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Egocentric human video is proposed as a scalable source of robot priors, with an open 50,000-hour recipe and two world–action models.

digest_headlines.heading: Building an Open Egocentric Pretraining Corpus
digest_headlines.headline: Open-HumanScale-50K draws on five sources, filters clips for hand visibility, motion stability, and activity, and aligns actions into one bimanual space.

digest_headlines.heading: Exploration of Pure Egocentric Data Scaling
digest_headlines.headline: Downstream success follows a log-linear law in pretraining hours, with larger gains under out-of-distribution shifts than in-distribution.

digest_headlines.heading: Pure Egocentric Data Foundation Model Training
digest_headlines.headline: After post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% on Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, below the leading entry's 81.48% on Clean2Random.

digest_headlines.heading: Pushing the Model Capability Boundary with Hybrid Data Scaling
digest_headlines.headline: Adding 45,938 hours of human video to a 14,618-hour robot corpus raises Random success from 70.80% to 74.36%, breaking the robot-only plateau.

digest_headlines.heading: Emerging Capabilities in Real-World Robot Behavior
digest_headlines.headline: Hybrid scaling raises real-robot zero-shot success from 20.0% to 30.5% across 20 tasks, and visual goals steer the frozen policy to different outcomes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work groups world–action models, pure egocentric pretraining, and in-context learning, and positions this study as scaling egocentric data across them.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Open-HumanScale reports a log-linear out-of-distribution scaling law from human video, and HumanWAM-Goal improves zero-shot and post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 transfer.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers goal image synthesis and review for RoboTwin, and the real-world zero-shot task suite with scoring rubrics.

repos.title: Transforming Integer Grids to Spatial Intuition: Perception, Not Planning, Governs ARC-AGI-3
repos.paper_summary: Sarbloh is an open-weight agent for ARC-AGI-3, an interactive game benchmark that penalizes extra actions quadratically. A parameter-free perception engine turns each frame, in about 35 ms, into tracked objects, a geometric briefing, and an annotated map. The briefing follows the Measured–Guessed Rule: computed relations such as reachability and symmetry are stated as facts, while object roles are stated as guesses, each with a one-action test. On a 28-point perception rubric, the fused briefing scored 25 against 3 for a text-only encoder, using 89.4% fewer tokens. On 23 held-out games, geometric invariants reached 100% spatial accuracy, while single-frame affordance guesses ranged from 6% to 50%. On 25 public games, Run A (briefing off) resolved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours with a median human action ratio of 0.77x; Run B (briefing on) reached 0.68x. The official hidden score was 16.53, 13.7x the first Milestone winner, within nine hours on one GPU. Limitations: hypotheses are checked frame by frame without a unified belief state, complex perceptual transitions cause most score loss, and no task-specific fine-tuning is used.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Raw integer grids make frontier models waste actions, and Sarbloh addresses this with grounded perception and code actions.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: ARC-AGI-3 gives colour grids and scores each level by action count, penalizing extra actions quadratically.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation: Perception as the Primary Bottleneck
digest_headlines.headline: Perception, not planning, limited a frontier model: raw grids cost 200 to 300 actions, code search cleared the level in 6.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Facts are computed exactly from the grid, while object roles are labeled as guesses with a test.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Perception lifts the rubric from 3 to 25 of 28, and the official hidden score reaches 16.53.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier interactive agents pass raw grids to the model, while Sarbloh computes geometric invariants on the host.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Limits: hypotheses are checked frame by frame without a unified belief, and no task-specific fine-tuning is used.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Perception, not planning, is argued to limit interactive reasoning, so structured perception can keep open-weight models efficient.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists notation, the scheduler, hyperparameters, lab protocols, failure modes, telemetry, and reproducible artifacts.
